    "thumbnail": "https://i.ytimg.com/vi/mDG_Hx3BSUE/maxresdefault.jpg",
    "description": "Dylan Patel, founder of SemiAnalysis, provides a deep dive into the 3 big bottlenecks to scaling AI compute: logic, memory, and power.\n\nAnd walks through the economics of labs, hyperscalers, foundries, and fab equipment manufacturers.\n\nLearned a ton about every single level of the stack. Enjoy!\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/dylan-patel\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/dylan-patel-deep-dive-on-the-3-big-bottlenecks-to/id1516093381?i=1000755126873\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/5qiibwoBWY5rXyflK7WJzH?si=SX4ajSKXT-KeNtaHsiTNzw\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Mercury has already saved me a bunch of time this tax season. Last year, I used Mercury to request W-9s from all the contractors I worked with. Then, when it came time to issue 1099s this year, I literally just clicked a button and Mercury sent them out. Learn more at https://mercury.com\n- Labelbox noticed that even when voice models appear to take interruptions in stride, their performance degrades. To figure out why, they built a new evaluation pipeline called EchoChain. EchoChain diagnoses voice models’ specific failure modes, letting you understand what your model needs to truly handle interruptions. Check it out at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n- Jane Street is basically a research lab with a trading desk attached – and their infrastructure backs this up. They’ve got tens of thousands of GPUs, hundreds of thousands of CPU cores, and exabytes of storage. This is what it takes to find subtle signals hidden deep within noisy market data. If this sounds interesting, you can explore open positions at https://janestreet.com/dwarkesh\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n00:00:00 – Why an H100 is worth more today than 3 years ago\n00:24:52 – Nvidia secured TSMC allocation early; Google is getting squeezed\n00:34:34 – ASML will be the #1 constraint for AI compute scaling by 2030\n00:55:47 – Can't we just use TSMC's older fabs?\n01:05:37 – When will China outscale the West in semis?\n01:16:01 – The enormous incoming memory crunch\n01:42:34 – Scaling power in the US will not be a problem\n01:54:44 – Space GPUs aren't happening this decade\n02:14:07 – Why aren't more hedge funds making the AGI trade?\n02:18:30 – Will TSMC kick Apple out from N2?\n02:24:16 – Robots and Taiwan risk",

      "id": "UgzL6LnjFnjbS2dcyLV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The Big Picture: AI Compute Economics\nThe Big Four hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft) have a combined $600 billion in forecasted CapEx this year, translating to roughly a trillion dollars across the full supply chain. Much of this isn't for compute coming online immediately — large chunks go toward turbine deposits, data center construction, and power purchasing agreements years into the future. About 20 gigawatts of new AI compute capacity is being added in the US this year.\nAnthropic vs. OpenAI: A Compute Arms Race\nThis is one of the episode's most interesting threads. Anthropic has been adding roughly $4–6 billion in revenue per month. At current gross margins, sustaining that growth requires adding around 4 gigawatts of inference capacity this year alone, pushing them toward needing 5+ gigawatts total by year-end. The problem: Dario was conservative on compute commitments, not wanting to risk bankruptcy. OpenAI, by contrast, signed aggressive long-term deals with CoreWeave, Oracle, SoftBank Energy, and others — even when the market doubted they could pay. Now that OpenAI has raised $110 billion, everyone's happy to work with them. Anthropic is having to scramble for capacity from lower-quality providers and pay premium spot rates (as high as $2.40/hour for H100s on multi-year deals, versus a $1.40 cost to deploy). They're also leaning on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry revenue-sharing arrangements. Dylan estimates both labs will end 2026 around 5–6 gigawatts each.\nWhy an H100 Is Worth More Today Than 3 Years Ago\nThis is counterintuitive. The bears argued GPU depreciation should be 2–3 years because newer chips keep coming. But Dylan makes the case that what prices a chip isn't what you could buy instead — it's the value you can extract from it today. GPT-5.4 is both cheaper to run and far more capable than GPT-4. An H100 running 5.4 produces more tokens of a higher-quality model, and the TAM for those tokens is orders of magnitude larger. In a semiconductor-constrained world, the value per GPU actually increases over time as models improve.\nThe Three Bottlenecks: Logic, Memory, and Power\nThe bottleneck keeps shifting. It was CoWoS packaging, then power and data centers. Now it's moving to the semiconductor supply chain itself — and staying there.\nLogic: Nvidia locked up TSMC's 3nm allocation early, well before Google or Amazon realized how much they'd need. Google made the mistake of selling a million TPU v7s to Anthropic before understanding their own demand was about to explode (Nano Banana and Gemini 3 caused user metrics to skyrocket). By the time Google went back to TSMC asking for more, TSMC was sold out. Nvidia now commands 70%+ of N3 capacity by 2027.\nMemory: This is the part of the episode that has the most striking consumer implications. HBM uses 4x the wafer area per gigabyte versus standard DRAM. As AI sucks up memory capacity, consumer devices get hammered. iPhone memory costs could increase by $100–150, and smartphone volumes could drop from 1.1 billion to 500–600 million units. About 30% of Big Tech's 2026 CapEx — roughly $180 billion — goes to memory. The memory vendors didn't build new fabs for years because prices were low and margins were terrible in 2023. Now fabs take two years to build. Pricing has already tripled and may double again. Dylan predicts people will hate AI more and more as their phones and PCs get more expensive.\nPower: Dylan is the most optimistic here. Combined-cycle gas turbines are just one of 16+ power generation technologies he tracks. Aeroderivative engines, reciprocating engines, ship engines, fuel cells (Bloom Energy), solar plus battery — any one of these can individually produce tens of gigawatts, and collectively hundreds. Even if behind-the-meter power costs 2x more than grid power, it only adds about $0.10/hour to GPU costs. The real constraint is labor (electricians, construction workers), which is being addressed through modularization — shipping pre-integrated megawatt-scale blocks from Asian factories.\nASML: The Ultimate Bottleneck\nBy 2028–2029, everything converges on ASML's EUV machines. They currently produce about 70 per year, growing to maybe 100 by decade's end. Each machine costs $300–400 million. You need roughly 3.5 EUV tools per gigawatt of AI compute (across logic and memory combined). So 700 cumulative tools by 2030 could theoretically support ~200 gigawatts — if it were all allocated to AI. Sam Altman's target of 52 gigawatts/year implies about 25% market share of total chip production, which Dylan considers reasonable.\nASML can't scale faster because the machine is the most complex thing humans manufacture at volume. The source drops tin droplets and hits them with a laser three times to generate 13.5nm light. Carl Zeiss makes 18 multilayer mirrors per tool with sub-nanometer precision. The reticle and wafer stages move at 9 Gs in opposite directions. The supply chain involves 10,000+ suppliers. ASML has been remarkably generous on pricing — never raising prices faster than capability improvements — despite having zero competition.\nChina\nDylan thinks China will have fully indigenized DUV by 2030 and working (but not mass-produced) EUV tools. They could manufacture ~100 DUV tools/year by then versus ASML's hundreds. His framework: fast AI timelines favor the US (the labs are scaling revenue and compute so fast that China can't keep up); slow timelines favor China (they can build a fully vertical supply chain). He notes that Huawei, if it had TSMC access, would arguably be better than Nvidia — they have superior AI researchers, networking technology, their own fabs, and their own end markets.\nSpace Data Centers\nDylan is quite skeptical for this decade. GPUs are unreliable (15% of Blackwells need RMA), and the test-deconstruct-launch-reassemble cycle adds months. Networking between satellites is far more expensive and less reliable than terrestrial fiber. Cooling is harder in space (you can't do exotic liquid cooling as easily). Most importantly, in a chip-constrained world, you want GPUs producing tokens the moment they're manufactured — any deployment delay destroys value. Space data centers might make sense in 2035+ once chips are no longer the binding constraint and energy/land permitting become dominant.\nRapid-Fire Highlights\n\nApple is getting squeezed out of TSMC. By the A16 node, AI — not Apple — will be the first and largest customer.\nTSMC prefers giving allocation to CPUs (Graviton, AMD EPYC) over AI accelerators because they view that business as more stable.\nModel architecture trends favor smaller, faster-to-RL models over giant ones, because the research feedback loop compounds faster.\nElon's TeraFab plan: Dylan thinks he can build the clean room but developing an actual process technology is a much harder, longer problem.\nThe \"AGI trade\": Leopold Aschenbrenner is the only SemiAnalysis client who consistently says their numbers are too low. Everyone else says they're too high. Six months later, the numbers prove right.\nTaiwan risk: If Taiwan's fabs were destroyed, global AI compute additions would collapse from hundreds of gigawatts/year to maybe 10–20, and GDP would shrink massively.",

      "text": "@2:30:02: This is why there isn't going to be a hot war over Taiwan.  If China invades, it'll be some soft thing, and the US will be faced with a choice between making it go hard, which will wreck the US and world economy, or negotiating some settlement in which China ends up with political control over Taiwan.  The US will choose the latter.\n\nNow the interesting bit is that US and Taiwanese interests diverge here.  If the Taiwanese fabs are wrecked, those Taiwanese engineers, and there are a HUGE number of them, become a critical resource for the world economy.  Those folks have agency!  The US can forcibly pull them out of Taiwan, I'm sure, but probably not their extended families and definitely not their homes.  If they're feeling stressed and distracted, they aren't going to be working at max efficiency, which is what everyone else would want to get the economy going again.  So this large very important class of people actually have a lot of political power, and they might want the US to make their home safe.  They'll communicate that before the fabs get wrecked.\n\nUnfortunately, China pretty much wins what it wants politically almost regardless of how it goes.  I say unfortunately not because I'd like to see China do worse (three cheers for the greatest expansion of human standard of living ever), but because I don't want China to do better at the expense of the rest of us.",

      "id": "UgzREUmEmGI5AF6p2EJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "@2:04:57: Here the two of them just launch right off the rails.\n\nChips are not cooling by radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann).  1 W/mm^2 is 1776 C -- nevermind about electromigration problems at 100+ C, the copper melts at 1085 C and you are way, way past that.\n\nThe problem with cooling high powered chips is not affected by being in outer space, except in the sense that high intensity cooling involves liquids, liquids involve plumbing, and plumbing inevitably leaks and requires plumbers.  So GPUs in space requires plumbers in space, and that's a problem.  But near the chip, cooling a GPU in space is exactly the same problem as cooling a GPU on the ground.\n\nAlso, immersion does not help, because there is not lots of excess area on the die which is not currently used to eject heat.  Greater cooling intensity requires phase change.  Phase change is difficult, because if there isn't a pressure gradient, then the liquid boils at the surface in contact with the hot die, and then the vapor insulates the remaining surface (the Leidenfrost effect).  To get phase change to work you need a pressure drop, so that the liquid picks up heat from the die by forced convection, then moves a distance which is an order of magnitude less than the size of the die (so, 1 mm or less), to a surface exposed to LOW PRESSURE vapor, at which point the liquid evaporates.  You need a structure like the stomata on plant leaves, which use surface tension at a very small scale to generate huge pressure gradients at a free surface.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCnjJ_XzSFLAIcQYQgjPsepw",
      "author": "@IainMcClatchie",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nMAY0M-PR5z85MfUK178CxrtHlIyyMe2bq31_16LwOTg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugzqdp8JAarswN8qORd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "@1:22:40: The model he's articulating is that communication happens through the shoreline of the chip.  This isn't quite right, and the way it's different matters to this discussion.\n\nThe chip has to move electricity in, heat out, and bits both ways.  Heat is most difficult, because silicon has a thermal conductivity of 150 W/m/K and we can tolerate at most 20 K drop on the way out, so 3000 W/m.  To think in the same units, assume the chip runs at 1 volt and can tolerate a 50 mV drop going in and out.  Copper then has an electrical conductivity of 3,000,000 W/m.  So, you need a thousand times more silicon to get the heat out as copper to get the power in.  What that means is you use the entire face of the chip to pull heat out, but you move electricity and bits in through the other face with little vias.  The wires carrying bits then generally turn sideways and run along the face of the interposer.  And, if we cut the interposer along the edge of the compute die mounted above it, we get Dylan's model of communication happening through the shoreline.\n\n2048 wires in 13 mm sounds like a lot.  It's about a 6 micron pitch for the wires if they were in a single level.  But it's important to realize that on-chip wiring is much smaller, and typically runs at 2 Gb/s rather than 10 Gb/s, and also that a bunch of the power dissipation on the compute die is from converting between those two speeds.  That on-chip wiring cannot run at reasonable speeds while passively carrying bits more than 1 mm or so.\n\nThat \"passively\" word is the clue.  Interposers today are passive.  If instead the interposers were fabricated on e.g. 22nm TSMC, you could have at least two layers of wiring at 100 nm pitch, running at 2 Gb/s, with inverters (burning power) every millimeter or so.  This would deliver 20-30 times as much bandwidth.  It would also burn power, but it would save power on both the compute and HBM dies.  Even better, it would save area on the compute die, as there would be no need for serdes blocks.\n\nThe usual objection is that a 22nm interposer has the same reticle-limited size as a compute die.  To overcome the problem, you assemble four interposer dies and connect the compute die as the junction of the four.  This adds a bunch of alignment constraints which I'm sure will take a bunch of smart people to solve, but it can be done.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCnjJ_XzSFLAIcQYQgjPsepw",
      "author": "@IainMcClatchie",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nMAY0M-PR5z85MfUK178CxrtHlIyyMe2bq31_16LwOTg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 month ago",

      "id": "UgzUOUznps8947KYWMJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I’m pulling the highest-signal sections rather than the most entertaining ones. A lot of this interview is repetitive, so the best half hour is not the first half hour.\n\nThought for 34s\n\nWatch these 5 clips. They give you the core thesis without wasting time on the weaker parts.\n\nBest 30-minute cut\n\n1) 6:50 to 10:21\nWhy old H100s got more expensive instead of cheaper\nThis is the cleanest explanation of the current compute market: short-term vs long-term contracts, why labs are bidding up old GPUs, and why “GPU depreciation” takes are too shallow.\n\n2) 12:09 to 15:51\nWhy an H100 can be worth more now than 3 years ago\nThis is the most important conceptual section in the whole interview. The claim is simple: the value of a GPU depends on the value models can extract from it, not just on newer hardware existing.\n\n3) 26:09 to 34:05\nHow Nvidia locked up TSMC and how Google got squeezed\nBest section on strategy and supply chain timing. If you want one clip that explains why Nvidia keeps winning, this is it. Also covers Google selling TPU capacity to Anthropic and realizing too late what it gave up.\n\n4) 37:11 to 45:54\nASML as the real long-run bottleneck\nThis is the deepest part of the conversation. It moves past “power is the bottleneck” and explains why EUV lithography may be the actual ceiling on AI compute by 2030.\n\n5) 1:21:04 to 1:26:48\nWhy HBM matters and why AI may make phones/PCs worse\nBest section on memory. It explains why commodity DRAM is not a real substitute, why HBM wins anyway, and why consumer electronics get squeezed.\n\nThat totals about 29 minutes 30 seconds.\n\nIf you want a more geopolitical version\n\nSwap out clip 5 for:\n\n1:05:42 to 1:15:50\nWhen China could catch up or overtake in semis\nThis is better if you care more about US vs China than memory economics.\n\nWhat to skip\n\nSkip most of the power and space GPUs sections unless you are specifically interested in infra buildout. They are interesting, but they are not the highest-signal parts of the interview. The real substance is compute contracts, TSMC allocation, ASML, and memory.\n\nIf you want, I can also turn this into a top 10 clip list ranked by signal-to-noise.",

      "id": "UgyXgpwU9MVQfIhGkYF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dylan is basically saying the story isn’t just “we need more GPUs.”  It’s that the bottleneck keeps moving.Better models can make older GPUs more valuable. Early long-term compute contracts suddenly look genius. Then the constraint moves from power/datacenters to manufacturing, maybe even EUV. That also makes the rest of the episode fit together better: HBM vs consumer devices, Apple/TSMC, space datacenters being too early, and Taiwan as the real tail risk. Not sure every number has to be right, but I think the overall framework is really good.",

      "author_id": "UCorR26oNE1-zrKdUkujJrJw",
      "author": "@sleepinpool",

      "text": "The power assumptions Dylan makes are an order of magnitude off. ## Description

Dylan Patel, founder of SemiAnalysis, provides a deep dive into the 3 big bottlenecks to scaling AI compute: logic, memory, and power.

And walks through the economics of labs, hyperscalers, foundries, and fab equipment manufacturers.

Learned a ton about every single level of the stack. Enjoy!

- Labelbox noticed that even when voice models appear to take interruptions in stride, their performance degrades. To figure out why, they built a new evaluation pipeline called EchoChain. EchoChain diagnoses voice models’ specific failure modes, letting you understand what your model needs to truly handle interruptions. Check it out at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh
- Jane Street is basically a research lab with a trading desk attached – and their infrastructure backs this up. one of which is higher quality and one which is&nbsp;&nbsp; lower quality, that will make people choose&nbsp; the higher quality good, on the margin.&nbsp; To give a specific example, suppose the&nbsp; better-tasting apple costs two dollars and&nbsp;&nbsp;

the shittier apple costs one dollar. Now suppose you put an import tariff on them.&nbsp; Now it's $3 versus $2 for a great&nbsp; apple versus a medium apple.&nbsp; Is that because they both increased by a&nbsp;

dollar, or should it be a 50% increase?&nbsp; No, because they both increased by $1. The whole effect is that if there's&nbsp;&nbsp; a fixed cost that is applied to both. Then the price difference between them,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the ratio, changes. Previously, the more&nbsp;&nbsp; expensive one was 2X more expensive. Now it's just 1.5X more expensive.&nbsp; So I wonder if applied to AI that would mean&nbsp;

that, if GPUs are going to get more expensive,&nbsp;&nbsp; there will be a fixed cost&nbsp; increase in the price of compute.&nbsp; As a result, that will push people to be willing&nbsp; to pay higher margins for slightly better models.&nbsp;

so you have to put chips in different racks. The movement of data between racks is on the order&nbsp;&nbsp; of hundreds of gigabits a second, 400 gig or 800&nbsp; gig a second, so roughly 100 gigabytes a second.&nbsp; So you have this huge ladder: on-chip&nbsp;

communication is super fast, within the&nbsp;&nbsp; rack is an order of magnitude slower, and outside&nbsp; the rack is an order of magnitude lower than that.&nbsp; As you break the bounds of chips,&nbsp; you end up with a performance loss.&nbsp;

The reason I explain this is because&nbsp; when you look at Hopper versus Blackwell,&nbsp;&nbsp; even if both are using a rack's worth of&nbsp; chips, Hopper is significantly slower.&nbsp; The amount of performance you have leveraged to&nbsp;

the task within each domain—tens of terabytes a&nbsp;&nbsp; second of communication between these processing&nbsp; elements versus terabytes a second between these&nbsp;&nbsp; processing elements—is much, much higher and&nbsp; therefore the performance is much higher.&nbsp;

When you look at inference at 100 tokens&nbsp; a second for DeepSeek and Kimi K2.5,&nbsp;&nbsp; the performance difference between Hopper&nbsp; and Blackwell is on the order of 20x.&nbsp; It's not 2x or 3x like the FLOPS&nbsp;

performance difference indicates,&nbsp;&nbsp; even though those are on the same process node. There are just differences in networking&nbsp;&nbsp; technologies and what they've worked on. You can translate some of these back,&nbsp;&nbsp;

but when you look at what they're doing&nbsp; on 3 nm with Rubin, some of those things&nbsp;&nbsp; are simply not possible to do all the way back&nbsp; on A100, even if you make a new chip for 7 nm.&nbsp; There are certain architectural improvements&nbsp;

you can port and certain ones you cannot.&nbsp; The performance difference is not just&nbsp; going to be the difference in FLOPS.&nbsp; It's in some senses cumulative between&nbsp; the difference in FLOPS per chip,&nbsp;&nbsp;

networking speed between chips, how many FLOPS&nbsp; are on a chip versus a system, and memory&nbsp;&nbsp; bandwidth on a single chip versus an entire&nbsp; system. All of these things compound.&nbsp; Can I ask you a very naive question?

up, there is some performance loss.&nbsp; It's not perfect, but it is way&nbsp; better than different entire packages.&nbsp; How large can advanced packaging scale? The way Nvidia is doing it is CoWoS.&nbsp;

of the I/O escapes on the edges. Often, the left and right of the&nbsp;&nbsp; chip are HBM—so the I/O from the chip&nbsp; to the HBM is on the sides—and then the&nbsp;&nbsp; top and bottom are I/O to other chips.

If you were to change from HBM to DDR,&nbsp;&nbsp; all of a sudden this I/O on the edge&nbsp; would have significantly less bandwidth,&nbsp;&nbsp; but significantly more capacity per chip. But the metric you actually care about&nbsp;&nbsp;

is bandwidth per wafer, not bits per wafer. Because the thing that is constraining the FLOPS&nbsp;&nbsp; is just getting in and out the next matrix,&nbsp; and for that you just need more bandwidth.&nbsp; Yeah, getting out the weights and&nbsp;

getting in and out the KV cache.&nbsp; In many cases, these GPUs are not&nbsp; running at full memory capacity.&nbsp; It's obviously a system design thing:&nbsp; model, hardware, and software co-design.&nbsp;

Obviously, the search space for this is very&nbsp;&nbsp; broad, which is why we have InferenceX,&nbsp; an open-source model that searches all&nbsp;&nbsp; the optimal points on inference for a&nbsp; variety of different chips and models.&nbsp;

The point is, you're not always&nbsp; necessarily constrained by memory capacity.&nbsp; You can be constrained by FLOPS, network&nbsp; bandwidth, memory bandwidth, or memory capacity.&nbsp; If you really simplify it down,&nbsp;

difference in bandwidth per edge area. If your chip is a square, or 26 by 33&nbsp;&nbsp; millimeters—which is the maximum size for an&nbsp; individual die—you only have so much edge area.&nbsp; On the inside of that chip,&nbsp;

go to 3D DRAM. That is the hope. Right now,&nbsp;&nbsp; everyone's roadmap goes from the current 6F cell,&nbsp; to a 4F cell, and then finally 3D DRAM by the end&nbsp;&nbsp; of the decade or early next decade. There's still a lot of R&amp;D,&nbsp;&nbsp;

manufacturing, and integration to be done. I wouldn't call that out of the cards.&nbsp; I think it's very likely going to happen. It's also going to require a huge&nbsp;&nbsp; retooling of fabs.

types of chemical vapor deposition, atomic layer&nbsp; deposition, dry etch, or different kinds of etch&nbsp;&nbsp; chambers with different chemistries… You have all&nbsp; these different tools for different process nodes.&nbsp; You can't just convert a logic fab to a&nbsp;

add DUV and change the chemistry stacks for when&nbsp; you’re using EUV in terms of deposition and etch.&nbsp; And the EUV tool has to be there. Furthermore, when you change to 3D DRAM,&nbsp;&nbsp; there's going to be an even larger shift, so a&nbsp;

likely cross into the 20% range.&nbsp; But then, if we get to 3D DRAM, the total end&nbsp; wafer cost as a percentage of EUV tanks again.&nbsp; I guess you care less about the percent of cost&nbsp; and more about how much it bottlenecks production.&nbsp;

Nvidia versus Trainium versus TPUs. Earlier I was mentioning how&nbsp;&nbsp; communication within a chip is super fast. Communication within chips that are in the&nbsp;&nbsp; same rack is fast, but not as fast.

It's on the order of terabytes.&nbsp; Communication very far away is on&nbsp; the order of hundreds of gigabytes.&nbsp; As you get further distance, maybe&nbsp; across the country, the order&nbsp;&nbsp;

of magnitude is on the order of gigabytes. A scale-up domain is this tight domain&nbsp;&nbsp; where the chips are communicating&nbsp; on the order of terabytes a second.&nbsp; For Nvidia, previously this meant&nbsp;

an H100 server had eight GPUs,&nbsp;&nbsp; and those eight GPUs could talk to&nbsp; each other at terabytes a second.&nbsp; With Blackwell NVL72, they&nbsp; implemented rack-scale scale-up.&nbsp;

That meant all seventy-two GPUs in the rack could&nbsp; connect to each other at terabytes a second.&nbsp; The speed doubled generation on generation, but&nbsp; the most important innovation was going from eight&nbsp;&nbsp; to seventy-two in the domain.

When we look at Google,&nbsp;&nbsp; their scale-up domain is completely different. It has always been on the order of thousands.&nbsp; With TPU v4, they had pods the&nbsp; size of four thousand chips.&nbsp;

With v8 or v7, they have pods in&nbsp; the eight or nine thousand range.&nbsp; What's relevant here is that it's not the&nbsp; same as Nvidia. It's not like for like.&nbsp;&nbsp; Google has a topology that's a torus.

Every chip connects to six neighbors.&nbsp;&nbsp; Nvidia's 72 GPUs connect all-to-all.&nbsp; They can send terabytes a second to&nbsp;&nbsp; any arbitrary other chip in that pod of scale-up. Whereas Google, you have to bounce through chips.&nbsp;

If TPU 1 needs to talk to TPU 76, it has to bounce&nbsp; through various chips, and there is always some&nbsp;&nbsp; blocking of resources when you do that because&nbsp; that one TPU is only connected to six other TPUs.&nbsp; So there is a difference&nbsp;

in topology and bandwidth,&nbsp;&nbsp; and there are trade-offs and advantages to both. Google gets to have a massive scale-up domain,&nbsp;&nbsp; but they have the trade-off of bouncing&nbsp; across chips to get from one to another.&nbsp;

You can only talk to six direct neighbors. Amazon has mutated their scale-up domain.&nbsp; They're somewhere in between Nvidia and Google. They're trying to make larger scale-up domains.&nbsp; They try to do all-to-all to some extent with&nbsp;

switches, which is what Nvidia does, but they also&nbsp;&nbsp; use torus topologies like Google to some extent. As we advance forward to next generations,&nbsp;&nbsp; all three of them are moving more&nbsp; towards a dragonfly topology.&nbsp;

That means there are some fully connected elements&nbsp; and some elements that are not fully connected.&nbsp; You can get the scale-up to be hundreds or&nbsp; thousands of chips, but also have it not contend&nbsp;&nbsp; for resources when bouncing through chips.

or maybe millions of instances—the future&nbsp; you're suggesting is one where there's more&nbsp;&nbsp; centralized thinking and centralized computation&nbsp; driving millions of robots out in the world.&nbsp; That's an interesting fact about the future&nbsp;

that I think people might not appreciate.&nbsp; I think Elon recognizes this, which is why&nbsp; he's going to different places for his chips.&nbsp; He signed this massive deal with Samsung to make&nbsp; his robot chips in Texas because I personally&nbsp;&nbsp;

think he thinks Taiwan risk is huge. Because of that and the centralization&nbsp;&nbsp; of resources in Taiwan, having his robot&nbsp; chips in Texas means having a separate&nbsp;&nbsp; supply chain that is not as constrained.

No one's really making AI chips on Samsung&nbsp;&nbsp; besides Nvidia's new LPU that they launched. They’re launching it next week, but we're&nbsp;&nbsp; recording this the week before. This episode's coming out Friday.&nbsp;

Oh, this episode's coming out before.&nbsp; Sick. They're launching this new AI chip&nbsp;&nbsp; next week which is built on Samsung, but&nbsp; that's a recent development from Nvidia.&nbsp; That's the only other AI demand there,&nbsp;

whereas on TSMC, everything is competing.&nbsp; He gets both geopolitical diversification&nbsp; and supply chain diversity for his robots,&nbsp;&nbsp; and he's not competing as much with the infinite&nbsp; willingness to pay for the data center geniuses.&nbsp;

Final question, on Taiwan. If we believe&nbsp; that tools are the ultimate bottleneck,&nbsp;&nbsp; how much of Taiwan's place in the AI semiconductor&nbsp; supply chain could we de-risk simply by having a&nbsp;&nbsp; plan to airlift every single process engineer&nbsp;

at TSMC out if they get blockaded or something?&nbsp; Or do you still need to ship out the EUV&nbsp; tools, which would be multiple plane loads&nbsp;&nbsp; per single tool and would not be practical? If you ship out all the process engineers and&nbsp;&nbsp;

assuming it's hot enough that you destroy the&nbsp; fabs, no one has all the fabs in Taiwan now,&nbsp;&nbsp; which is a big risk. These tools actually use a lot of&nbsp;&nbsp; semiconductors which are manufactured in Taiwan.

It's a snake eating its own tail meme because&nbsp;&nbsp; you can't make the tools without the chips from&nbsp; Taiwan, which you can't use without the tools in&nbsp;&nbsp; Taiwan. There's obviously some diversification&nbsp; there. They don't use super advanced chips in&nbsp;&nbsp;

lithography tools, but at the end of the&nbsp; day, there is some dragon eating its tail.&nbsp; Just shipping out all the engineers and&nbsp; blowing up the fabs means China has a&nbsp;&nbsp; stronger semiconductor supply chain than the&nbsp;

rest of the world in terms of verticalization,&nbsp;&nbsp; now that you've removed Taiwan. You've got all the know-how,&nbsp;&nbsp; but you've got to replicate it in,&nbsp; let's say, Arizona or wherever for TSMC.&nbsp;

It's going to take a long time to build all the&nbsp; capacity that TSMC has built over the years.&nbsp; And so you've drastically&nbsp; slowed US and global GDP.&nbsp; Not just growth, you've shrunk the GDP&nbsp;

massively, and you've got a lot bigger problems.&nbsp; Your incremental ability to add&nbsp; compute goes to almost zero.&nbsp; Instead of hundreds of gigawatts&nbsp; a year by the end of the decade,&nbsp;&nbsp;

let's say something happens to Taiwan, now you're&nbsp; at maybe 10 gigawatts across Intel and Samsung,&nbsp;&nbsp; or 20 gigawatts. It's nothing. Now all of a sudden&nbsp; you've really caused some crazy dynamics in AI.&nbsp; Of course, you have all the existing capacity,&nbsp;

> The Big Picture: AI Compute Economics
> The Big Four hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft) have a combined $600 billion in forecasted CapEx this year, translating to roughly a trillion dollars across the full supply chain. Much of this isn't for compute coming online immediately — large chunks go toward turbine deposits, data center construction, and power purchasing agreements years into the future. About 20 gigawatts of new AI compute capacity is being added in the US this year.
> Anthropic vs. OpenAI: A Compute Arms Race
> This is one of the episode's most interesting threads. Anthropic has been adding roughly $4–6 billion in revenue per month. At current gross margins, sustaining that growth requires adding around 4 gigawatts of inference capacity this year alone, pushing them toward needing 5+ gigawatts total by year-end. The problem: Dario was conservative on compute commitments, not wanting to risk bankruptcy. OpenAI, by contrast, signed aggressive long-term deals with CoreWeave, Oracle, SoftBank Energy, and others — even when the market doubted they could pay. Now that OpenAI has raised $110 billion, everyone's happy to work with them. Anthropic is having to scramble for capacity from lower-quality providers and pay premium spot rates (as high as $2.40/hour for H100s on multi-year deals, versus a $1.40 cost to deploy). They're also leaning on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry revenue-sharing arrangements. Dylan estimates both labs will end 2026 around 5–6 gigawatts each.
> Why an H100 Is Worth More Today Than 3 Years Ago
> This is counterintuitive. The bears argued GPU depreciation should be 2–3 years because newer chips keep coming. But Dylan makes the case that what prices a chip isn't what you could buy instead — it's the value you can extract from it today. GPT-5.4 is both cheaper to run and far more capable than GPT-4. An H100 running 5.4 produces more tokens of a higher-quality model, and the TAM for those tokens is orders of magnitude larger. In a semiconductor-constrained world, the value per GPU actually increases over time as models improve.
> The Three Bottlenecks: Logic, Memory, and Power
> The bottleneck keeps shifting. It was CoWoS packaging, then power and data centers. Now it's moving to the semiconductor supply chain itself — and staying there.
> Logic: Nvidia locked up TSMC's 3nm allocation early, well before Google or Amazon realized how much they'd need. Google made the mistake of selling a million TPU v7s to Anthropic before understanding their own demand was about to explode (Nano Banana and Gemini 3 caused user metrics to skyrocket). By the time Google went back to TSMC asking for more, TSMC was sold out. Nvidia now commands 70%+ of N3 capacity by 2027.
> Memory: This is the part of the episode that has the most striking consumer implications. HBM uses 4x the wafer area per gigabyte versus standard DRAM. As AI sucks up memory capacity, consumer devices get hammered. iPhone memory costs could increase by $100–150, and smartphone volumes could drop from 1.1 billion to 500–600 million units. About 30% of Big Tech's 2026 CapEx — roughly $180 billion — goes to memory. The memory vendors didn't build new fabs for years because prices were low and margins were terrible in 2023. Now fabs take two years to build. Pricing has already tripled and may double again. Dylan predicts people will hate AI more and more as their phones and PCs get more expensive.
> Power: Dylan is the most optimistic here. Combined-cycle gas turbines are just one of 16+ power generation technologies he tracks. Aeroderivative engines, reciprocating engines, ship engines, fuel cells (Bloom Energy), solar plus battery — any one of these can individually produce tens of gigawatts, and collectively hundreds. Even if behind-the-meter power costs 2x more than grid power, it only adds about $0.10/hour to GPU costs. The real constraint is labor (electricians, construction workers), which is being addressed through modularization — shipping pre-integrated megawatt-scale blocks from Asian factories.
> ASML: The Ultimate Bottleneck
> By 2028–2029, everything converges on ASML's EUV machines. They currently produce about 70 per year, growing to maybe 100 by decade's end. Each machine costs $300–400 million. You need roughly 3.5 EUV tools per gigawatt of AI compute (across logic and memory combined). So 700 cumulative tools by 2030 could theoretically support ~200 gigawatts — if it were all allocated to AI. Sam Altman's target of 52 gigawatts/year implies about 25% market share of total chip production, which Dylan considers reasonable.
> ASML can't scale faster because the machine is the most complex thing humans manufacture at volume. The source drops tin droplets and hits them with a laser three times to generate 13.5nm light. Carl Zeiss makes 18 multilayer mirrors per tool with sub-nanometer precision. The reticle and wafer stages move at 9 Gs in opposite directions. The supply chain involves 10,000+ suppliers. ASML has been remarkably generous on pricing — never raising prices faster than capability improvements — despite having zero competition.
> China
> Dylan thinks China will have fully indigenized DUV by 2030 and working (but not mass-produced) EUV tools. They could manufacture ~100 DUV tools/year by then versus ASML's hundreds. His framework: fast AI timelines favor the US (the labs are scaling revenue and compute so fast that China can't keep up); slow timelines favor China (they can build a fully vertical supply chain). He notes that Huawei, if it had TSMC access, would arguably be better than Nvidia — they have superior AI researchers, networking technology, their own fabs, and their own end markets.
> Space Data Centers
> Dylan is quite skeptical for this decade. GPUs are unreliable (15% of Blackwells need RMA), and the test-deconstruct-launch-reassemble cycle adds months. Networking between satellites is far more expensive and less reliable than terrestrial fiber. Cooling is harder in space (you can't do exotic liquid cooling as easily). Most importantly, in a chip-constrained world, you want GPUs producing tokens the moment they're manufactured — any deployment delay destroys value. Space data centers might make sense in 2035+ once chips are no longer the binding constraint and energy/land permitting become dominant.
> Rapid-Fire Highlights
> 
> Apple is getting squeezed out of TSMC. By the A16 node, AI — not Apple — will be the first and largest customer.
> TSMC prefers giving allocation to CPUs (Graviton, AMD EPYC) over AI accelerators because they view that business as more stable.
> Model architecture trends favor smaller, faster-to-RL models over giant ones, because the research feedback loop compounds faster.
> Elon's TeraFab plan: Dylan thinks he can build the clean room but developing an actual process technology is a much harder, longer problem.
> The "AGI trade": Leopold Aschenbrenner is the only SemiAnalysis client who consistently says their numbers are too low. Everyone else says they're too high. Six months later, the numbers prove right.
> Taiwan risk: If Taiwan's fabs were destroyed, global AI compute additions would collapse from hundreds of gigawatts/year to maybe 10–20, and GDP would shrink massively.

> @2:04:57: Here the two of them just launch right off the rails.
> 
> Chips are not cooling by radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann).  1 W/mm^2 is 1776 C -- nevermind about electromigration problems at 100+ C, the copper melts at 1085 C and you are way, way past that.
> 
> The problem with cooling high powered chips is not affected by being in outer space, except in the sense that high intensity cooling involves liquids, liquids involve plumbing, and plumbing inevitably leaks and requires plumbers.  So GPUs in space requires plumbers in space, and that's a problem.  But near the chip, cooling a GPU in space is exactly the same problem as cooling a GPU on the ground.
> 
> Also, immersion does not help, because there is not lots of excess area on the die which is not currently used to eject heat.  Greater cooling intensity requires phase change.  Phase change is difficult, because if there isn't a pressure gradient, then the liquid boils at the surface in contact with the hot die, and then the vapor insulates the remaining surface (the Leidenfrost effect).  To get phase change to work you need a pressure drop, so that the liquid picks up heat from the die by forced convection, then moves a distance which is an order of magnitude less than the size of the die (so, 1 mm or less), to a surface exposed to LOW PRESSURE vapor, at which point the liquid evaporates.  You need a structure like the stomata on plant leaves, which use surface tension at a very small scale to generate huge pressure gradients at a free surface.

- comment_id: Ugzqdp8JAarswN8qORd4AaABAg

> @1:22:40: The model he's articulating is that communication happens through the shoreline of the chip.  This isn't quite right, and the way it's different matters to this discussion.
> 
> The chip has to move electricity in, heat out, and bits both ways.  Heat is most difficult, because silicon has a thermal conductivity of 150 W/m/K and we can tolerate at most 20 K drop on the way out, so 3000 W/m.  To think in the same units, assume the chip runs at 1 volt and can tolerate a 50 mV drop going in and out.  Copper then has an electrical conductivity of 3,000,000 W/m.  So, you need a thousand times more silicon to get the heat out as copper to get the power in.  What that means is you use the entire face of the chip to pull heat out, but you move electricity and bits in through the other face with little vias.  The wires carrying bits then generally turn sideways and run along the face of the interposer.  And, if we cut the interposer along the edge of the compute die mounted above it, we get Dylan's model of communication happening through the shoreline.
> 
> 2048 wires in 13 mm sounds like a lot.  It's about a 6 micron pitch for the wires if they were in a single level.  But it's important to realize that on-chip wiring is much smaller, and typically runs at 2 Gb/s rather than 10 Gb/s, and also that a bunch of the power dissipation on the compute die is from converting between those two speeds.  That on-chip wiring cannot run at reasonable speeds while passively carrying bits more than 1 mm or so.
> 
> That "passively" word is the clue.  Interposers today are passive.  If instead the interposers were fabricated on e.g. 22nm TSMC, you could have at least two layers of wiring at 100 nm pitch, running at 2 Gb/s, with inverters (burning power) every millimeter or so.  This would deliver 20-30 times as much bandwidth.  It would also burn power, but it would save power on both the compute and HBM dies.  Even better, it would save area on the compute die, as there would be no need for serdes blocks.
> 
> The usual objection is that a 22nm interposer has the same reticle-limited size as a compute die.  To overcome the problem, you assemble four interposer dies and connect the compute die as the junction of the four.  This adds a bunch of alignment constraints which I'm sure will take a bunch of smart people to solve, but it can be done.

> I’m pulling the highest-signal sections rather than the most entertaining ones. A lot of this interview is repetitive, so the best half hour is not the first half hour.
> 
> Thought for 34s
> 
> Watch these 5 clips. They give you the core thesis without wasting time on the weaker parts.
> 
> Best 30-minute cut
> 
> 1) 6:50 to 10:21
> Why old H100s got more expensive instead of cheaper
> This is the cleanest explanation of the current compute market: short-term vs long-term contracts, why labs are bidding up old GPUs, and why “GPU depreciation” takes are too shallow.
> 
> 2) 12:09 to 15:51
> Why an H100 can be worth more now than 3 years ago
> This is the most important conceptual section in the whole interview. The claim is simple: the value of a GPU depends on the value models can extract from it, not just on newer hardware existing.
> 
> 3) 26:09 to 34:05
> How Nvidia locked up TSMC and how Google got squeezed
> Best section on strategy and supply chain timing. If you want one clip that explains why Nvidia keeps winning, this is it. Also covers Google selling TPU capacity to Anthropic and realizing too late what it gave up.
> 
> 4) 37:11 to 45:54
> ASML as the real long-run bottleneck
> This is the deepest part of the conversation. It moves past “power is the bottleneck” and explains why EUV lithography may be the actual ceiling on AI compute by 2030.
> 
> 5) 1:21:04 to 1:26:48
> Why HBM matters and why AI may make phones/PCs worse
> Best section on memory. It explains why commodity DRAM is not a real substitute, why HBM wins anyway, and why consumer electronics get squeezed.
> 
> That totals about 29 minutes 30 seconds.
> 
> If you want a more geopolitical version
> 
> Swap out clip 5 for:
> 
> 1:05:42 to 1:15:50
> When China could catch up or overtake in semis
> This is better if you care more about US vs China than memory economics.
> 
> What to skip
> 
> Skip most of the power and space GPUs sections unless you are specifically interested in infra buildout. They are interesting, but they are not the highest-signal parts of the interview. The real substance is compute contracts, TSMC allocation, ASML, and memory.
> 
> If you want, I can also turn this into a top 10 clip list ranked by signal-to-noise.
